articles.summary: AI is driving a boom in modestly successful software projects

blocks.text: If AI is so great, why aren’t we seeing an explosion of new, amazing software products? If anyone can turn their idea into working software with coding agents, where is all that software? People have been asking this question for years. As far as I can tell, the answer is that it’s spread out over a lot of modestly successful projects:
Somewhere between 2x and 20x new software is being created, depending on where you look
There’s no real growth in massively successful software projects (not counting AI tools)
There is around 2x growth in modestly successful software projects
Where all the new software is

I picked1 around twenty separate sources — software marketplaces, plugin registries, modding platforms, etc — which expose installation counts. I then compared the number2 of successful software projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26: i.e. before and after agentic coding hit the mainstream in mid-2025.

There’s a clear jump in modestly (not wildly) successful projects. For instance, the NVDA screen-reader addons directory had a bit over twice as many new addons with more than a thousand downloads (though no change in addons with more than ten thousand). The HACS open-source home automation community plugins store likewise saw twice as many new addons with over a hundred installs but no change in ones with over a thousand. New Steam games with over a hundred reviews are about 60% more common now than pre-2024. Obsidian plugins, Firefox and Chrome extensions, Nexus game mods, and Blender extensions had the same pattern. The Google Play store, WordPress plugins, and a few others didn’t show this pattern, but I think it’s still enough to conclude that AI is indeed driving a boom in hobbyist software.
Why addons and plugins?

I think examining addons, mods, and plugins is useful for a few reasons. First, it’s usually pretty easy to tell how many people are using them, or at least have installed them. Obviously AI is letting people produce a lot of software — I work at GitHub, so I see this first-hand, but the explosion in vibe-coded repos is clear to everyone — but without checking installation counts it’s unclear how much of this is actually being used.

Second, it’s a good way to minimize the amount of software that’s about AI. It doesn’t tell us much about AI’s effect on software to point out all the successful software projects that help people code with AI. That’s just selling shovels. The real question is whether AI is helping generate software that solves people’s ordinary problems.

AI-generated game mods and ports are a great example of this, because gamers aren’t trying to change the world with AI coding. They just want to play multiplayer Halo CE in the browser, or fly a plane in Helldivers, or play Super Smash online with rollback netcode. It’s looking like3 AI can supply this need effectively.
Were these projects actually AI generated?

Everyone is very coy about AI usage in hobbyist communities. In the rare cases where people admit it, they often get dogpiled. People really don’t like AI, even when it’s producing software they find useful. Given that, I don’t think it’s possible to use voluntary AI disclosure data to figure out whether AI is driving a software boom: the presence of the tag itself will discourage use, and many developers are just not going to admit it.

A 2x growth in successful projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26 is clearly something to do with AI, particularly in the background of a 10x growth in total projects. Of course not all of these projects will have AI involvement. But when people ask “why hasn’t AI improved software”, they’re talking about a missing trend4: wondering where all the new software is. As it turns out, it’s going towards a lot of small software projects that a few hundred or thousand people find useful.
Why small, moderately successful projects?

Why is AI growth visible in small projects but not big software companies? Why is it concentrated in moderately successful products and not wildly successful ones? I don’t have any data for this, but here’s my speculation.

Big, successful software companies often have all the visible features they want That’s why there’s not a wild explosion of new features in, say, macOS or Gmail: what would those features even be? As I’ve written about before, they’re also technically paralyzed by the features they have, so it’s not trivial for even very good coding agents to add new ones.  Finally, many new features in successful products are subtle (e.g. enterprise compatibility things that almost all users will never encounter, or purely internal systems that slightly increase reliability).

It’s less clear to me why there aren’t many new wildly successful hobbyist projects. Maybe it’s just hard to have a really good idea for a product, and AI can’t help with that. Or maybe it takes years for a really successful project to develop, and we need to be patient for the current crop of thousand-user tools to grow into hundred-thousand-user tools.

As you might expect, this research was all done with the help of AI. It wasn’t purely vibed — I gave a lot of feedback about where and how to look — but I would definitely not have scraped or analyzed this much data on my own. If you want to see the actual research data (or more likely point an agent at it), I’ve pushed it here.
↩

Sometimes scaling to take into account platform growth. For instance, between the two windows I measured, Obsidian relaxed their requirement that all new plugins be reviewed by an admin, which predictably caused an explosion of plugins on the marketplace.
↩

It certainly seems like it can so far, but who knows. Maybe once the hype has died down people will return to less buggy artisanal human-made mods and ports.
↩

They might also be asking “why hasn’t the software I use gotten better?” For that, see my thoughts in the final section of this post.

blocks.text:
October 11, 2026 / 10:31 AM EDT
            / CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
The following is the full transcript of the interview with Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 11, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by the Chief Technology Officer of Palantir, Shyam Sankar. Welcome to Face the Nation.
SHYAM SANKAR: Thank you for having me, Margaret.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It's good to have you here in person. We've been talking a lot about technology, artificial intelligence, and public perception of it right now, and that's where I want to start with you because our polling shows there's a problem here. 50% of those polled by CBS say AI will create more problems than it solves. 29% say it'll solve more than it creates, and 21% just really don't know. Like 45% of Americans want the government to restrict use and development of AI. Is your position there should not be any guardrails at this moment?

SHYAM SANKAR: No, not at all. That's not my position. I think the- the burden is absolutely on the technology industry to show the American people that there are real benefits to AI and not kind of ephemeral sort of benefits like it can help me schedule travel, but actually meaningful benefits that result in job growth and prosperity for the American people. I think one of the things that's really complicated in the current discussion, is that there's an unseen force driving the narrative around AI safety, and it's- it's really this millenarian doomsday cult meets messianic complex called effective altruism. The most famous effective altruist that most Americans know is Sam Bankman-Fried, and the effective altruists are, it's almost like a religion that they've been thinking about doomsday scenarios from AI since the early 2000s.
MARGARET BRENNAN:  He was–he is jailed. He was the crypto investor—
SHYAM SANKAR: Correct.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who defrauded investors. But this sounds very academic. Like, what makes you so focused on this?

SHYAM SANKAR:  Because there's only really roughly 2,000 AI researchers in America, and the vast majority of them believe in this sort of worldview around effective altruism. And if you hear someone like Jacob Coxon telling you that AI has a 10% chance of ending humanity, and you believe—
MARGARET BRENNAN:  A researcher who had this warning recently.

SHYAM SANKAR: Yes, correct. And you believe he's speaking as a technically informed individual who does this work, it's a scientific critique. I think the American people would be right to be quite panicked and worried about what's going on here. But if you understand that it's actually a theological critique, then you can- you can kind of weigh it against the empirical facts of what is actually happening out there. You know, I take—I think there's a profound truth to Pascal's saying that every human has a god-shaped hole in their heart, and it's important to understand that many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine God of AGI. And I mean, there's so many interesting stories around this. Like, for example, so many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI. I believe so much— (CROSSTALK)
MARGARET BRENNAN:  What? That makes no sense. What do you think—

SHYAM SANKAR: I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I will—I'm showing you my chips are all in. So there is kind of this mass psychosis, social delusion around it, and I think it's getting in the way of actually what is happening with AI. Where is it meeting the American worker in industry? What are the results of doing that, and the doomsdayers have basically been wrong. Everything they predicted, they- they told us that ChatGPT 2.0 was too dangerous to release. They told us at this point in the timeline, we'd already have mass unemployment and job displacement, and the economists see that actually we're having job growth in areas that we wouldn't have predicted doing exactly that. So the technology industry has two burdens. One is to show very clearly to the American people that- that AI is going to result in economic prosperity and security for the nation. And two, to actually do and absorb the burden of engineering. You cannot abdicate this idea that designing safe products is your job. You can't hand wave around it. If you look at the kind of narratives that come out of the doomsdayers, they seem like two contradictory narratives. One narrative is this technology is going to end humanity.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

SHYAM SANKAR: And simultaneously, they say, "But I believe it has some chance of creating utopia." So at first blush, this seems contradictory, but it has one thing in common, which is that you, as a human, have no agency. The machine god is going to decide the future, and only perhaps a small number of us can try to avoid the horrible outcome. And I think it obfuscates the more profound reality that we have a huge amount of human agency over how we're going to use this technology to deliver the outcomes the American people expect.

MARGARET BRENNAN:  Well let's talk about that because the other part of this argument would be, and no one who wants- the people who don't want guardrails are simply in it for commercial reasons. They want to keep selling chips, or they just want access to market. So that would be the counter argument to the idea that you know what you're saying, which is an ideological opposition to guardrails.
SHYAM SANKAR: Maybe we could just back up and who's on the side of no guardrails?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when- I want to get into the specifics here, because even just defining what guardrails is seems really complicated, and there's not even common agreement on that right now. But Jay Clayton, who is the new DNI and the new AI czar, said this week the focus is on control and monitoring of technologies with the potential to do harm. So, what does that look like to you? Because it sounds like he's not even sure yet.

SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I think there's a very clear view that we should be regulating the application of the technology. So if you're going to use this in medicines, you know the FDA- As a republic, we have 250 years of rich laws and history on how to manage liability. I don't want to trivialize the metaphor, but you know, if I buy a car and the car is defective, that's the car maker's problem. If I then use that car to go drive into my neighbor's house, that's my problem. And you know, this sort of obfuscation. The narrative is this technology is a total difference of kind. I don't think so. I think it's a difference of degree.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, in that humans aren't in control of it, it would be a different kind.

SHYAM SANKAR: No, humans are in control of it. Even if we look at the kind of salacious reporting around Hugging Face, the models did not do anything they were not instructed to do. You know, they were- the- the real first, you have human error. They- they were not in a sandbox. They had access to the internet. It was a horrible cybersecurity configuration. Then, from that perspective, they were asked to- to- succeed at a specific benchmark, and they were not given constraints on how to do that. And they said, "Oh, the best way to succeed at the benchmark is to get the answers to the test, and to do so.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, for that, who should take action to--
SHYAM SANKAR: --I think it's a defective product. Like, if--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Is it up to the Justice Department to then bring suit, like on the programmers, like who's liable for the technology not, you know, staying within the sandbox--

SHYAM SANKAR: --The AI companies of course. In that, in that specific case, it would be the AI companies. If another company had licensed that technology to use in another in an application, and the product worked as expected, but you misused the product, then it would be you that are responsible for that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you believe that, am I understanding you, the existing laws on the books should be able to handle technology as it develops?

SHYAM SANKAR: I think it is a massive running head start. I think the laws on the books speak to a lot of the current considerations. Might we need a few more things on the margin? Sure, but I think we'll figure that out as we go through it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So let's talk about some of those things because you were with the president when he summoned some of these AI leaders recently, and he asked them all to sign a pledge to implement robust internal controls, partner with an external auditor and establish a committee to evaluate reports from auditors. That was Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia, Elon Musk. They all signed it. Palantir, your company didn't. Why?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, those accords were for companies that actually make AI models, which we do not, so–
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you help to use them and build out platforms. Like you don't see a reason for constraints there.

SHYAM SANKAR: Oh, we- we do have those constraints. In fact, that- part of that's our entire business, is how do you safely deploy these models in specific use cases. We're just not a party that- we weren't asked to be a part of the accord.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you were there at that meeting.
SHYAM SANKAR: I was.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, what happened? Like, what was the conversation?

SHYAM SANKAR: The conversation was really an assertion that the American people expect AI to generate economic prosperity and to do so securely, and that we as companies have an affirmative obligation to deliver on exactly those things, and that we have existing laws to look at this, and that we should be all taking this quite seriously, very productive conversation.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because it sounded like the White House was saying something more should be done, and now you have this new AI Czar Jay Clayton going out to Silicon Valley this week. He said he's launched this 120-day review of AI policy. What do you hope comes from that, or is this another one of these like blue ribbon commissions that doesn't produce any--

SHYAM SANKAR: --No, I think a lot will come up to it, which is really focus and energy, and using the existing agencies and regulatory apparatus to make sure we're on top of this stuff and providing support where it's needed. I think one of the challenges, going back to my comments on effective altruism is, today, the so-called independent research organizations that are overseeing this are not really independent. They have conflicts with the labs. They are made up of people with a singular worldview around effective altruism, looking for the doomsday scenarios. You know, you have evaluators who are essentially pointing a loaded gun at a target, saying, "I can't believe the gun worked." When they should really be saying, "What guardrails do we have in place? You know- are you know are these products working to the specifications we designed, and what- what are the opportunities for misuse?

MARGARET BRENNAN: So I've spoken to people, for example, in the financial industry who say we did need some regulation here, but there's the SEC, there is you know the CFTC, they oversee certain operations here. Don't you think within the current institutions there could be some sort of entity that oversees technology?

SHYAM SANKAR: I think there's going to need to be an incident response and reporting regime that creates more visibility and transparency into what you're learning in the testing, well ahead of product launches that give visibility and transparency to the government of how people are doing and implementing exactly the existing laws.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who does that, or who could do that?
SHYAM SANKAR: I will defer to Director Clayton on that, but I think that's one of the things that I- I suspect they will be driving towards.

MARGARET BRENNAN: He's got to figure that out. Well, we look at the last administration- President Biden and Xi Jinping came to like, a very limited agreement, but at least on one principle, which was humans, not AI, should retain control over decisions to use nuclear weapons. Would it be sensible--
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, that seems obvious.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, that seems terrifying, first of all, that they had to come to a conversation about that, but shouldn't that be expanded elsewhere in the defense space? Would you agree with that? Is that one of the areas--

SHYAM SANKAR: Well, the current part of the policy is there's two parts of it. There's the kind of military doctrine, which is that a human is always accountable for every decision that's made, and the other part of it is that humans are in- in the decision-making processes that- that relate to lethal force here.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But in terms of the things where you think there should be more guardrails, is the defense space one of them? Biotech, I've heard others.
SHYAM SANKAR: All spaces need to- need to have a thought around safety of application.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But that's still- who does that and how?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I think the Department and the Congress should do it with defense. The Department of Transportation should do it with transportation. The FDA should do it with medicines.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But so, watch for that possibly happen. Because you know, I hear from people in the technology space this argument that we need to just go so furiously forward to compete with China. China is pushing for AI to be integrated into all of its industries, but they have the ability to also delay things to get government- governance to catch up, they've done that. They've tapped the brakes themselves before. So, do you think the U.S. should also consider tapping the brakes in certain areas, just slow things until they have some idea of the guardrails?

SHYAM SANKAR: You know, we have this beautiful, messy process in America, but I would argue, as frustrating as it might look, it's kind of working. So, we have frontier models now that have not been released because people have realized maybe we're not ready to release them. That would have been an unimaginable thought a year ago. And so as people are starting to wrap their heads around whether it's the labs, government- I think it is a consequence of our messy process and the discussions that people are having that we're evolving how we're doing this, and the pace is naturally changing.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let's talk a little bit about DOD, the Department of War, Department of Defense. They have recently ceased using Anthropic products as part of this dispute over the firm's insistence on safeguards for military use of AI. I know you're aware of this case. Anthropic's Claude was part of the Maven platform, which Palantir uses. How much of an impact will this decision here have, and who replaces them?

SHYAM SANKAR: Well, the- the Department today has a wide range of model providers, everything from XAI and OpenAI to open-weight models like Nemotron from NVIDIA, so I don't think- I don't- there's been no operational impact from that. I think there's a kind of a broader statement which really has been powering the growth of our commercial business, which is companies are realizing, and it equally applies to the government, that you're not going to pick any one model provider. That actually, your sovereignty and agency as an institution comes down to your ability to kind of control, decide which models you're going to use in what context, have the ability to switch models, to be able to control the weights themselves, where you need to feel that control over them. It is your alpha. It is what makes your institution special.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you don't know yet who's going to replace them, but you don't see a big impact from this kind of decision. It was certainly a huge story for Silicon Valley and the defense space to hear that--

SHYAM SANKAR: It's already been replaced. It's already been replaced, and users who are building AI applications get to pick the models that they're using. It's a suite of models that are available from, you know, Google, from XAI, from OpenAI. And what was the second part of your question there, sorry?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, I was asking about the impact. It sounds like you don't think it's- it's a big one. Look, I can move on here.
SHYAM SANKAR: No impact.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You have said recently that the war in Iran is the first major conflict where AI played a central role, particularly for targeting. Do you see risks for that?

SHYAM SANKAR: Well, you know, targeting is this- is kind of this very salacious word. Really, targeting is a process, and if you think about military operations, you know, the ability to execute 1000 strikes in a single day would have taken two weeks of planning by 50 people before, and being able to do that with one person in four hours provides you a significant battlefield advantage against your adversaries. So, it's really not about, you know, people jump immediately to something like AI picking the targets. That's not what's happening. It's really given a set of effects that you want to create- I want to be able to take out the enemy's air defenses. Okay, what targets relate to that? Okay, how do I then push them through a process where I understand are any of these targets on the no-strike list? Are any of these targets too close to civilian infrastructure? How do you do all the things that are so susceptible to human error under the time crunch- what's doing in a way that has much higher repeatability and accuracy, so you can get more throughput to the system?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, that goes to a broader argument about the elimination of some of the people who were involved in mitigating civilian impact from strikes. That was a Pentagon decision by Secretary Hegseth. In the case- you just talked about the thousands of strikes, and there were so many successful strikes in terms of the targeting in Iran. But there was also, as you know, this horrific one in Minab that killed at least 123 schoolchildren. Bloomberg reported some personnel relied too much on the AI in the Maven system made by Palantir using AI-enabled software. Have you determined what happened there?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, we should wait for the final report. But what I can say is that reporting is inaccurate.
MARGARET BRENNAN: The reporting from Bloomberg, you're saying, is inaccurate?

SHYAM SANKAR: Yeah, it's inaccurate, and actually, the likely cause is human error. And then- and quickly following that, we actually built additional AI agents that did more checking. The following is the full transcript of the interview with Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 11, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by the Chief Technology Officer of Palantir, Shyam Sankar. Welcome to Face the Nation.
SHYAM SANKAR: Thank you for having me, Margaret.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It's good to have you here in person. We've been talking a lot about technology, artificial intelligence, and public perception of it right now, and that's where I want to start with you because our polling shows there's a problem here. 50% of those polled by CBS say AI will create more problems than it solves. 29% say it'll solve more than it creates, and 21% just really don't know. Like 45% of Americans want the government to restrict use and development of AI. Is your position there should not be any guardrails at this moment?

SHYAM SANKAR: No, not at all. That's not my position. I think the- the burden is absolutely on the technology industry to show the American people that there are real benefits to AI and not kind of ephemeral sort of benefits like it can help me schedule travel, but actually meaningful benefits that result in job growth and prosperity for the American people. I think one of the things that's really complicated in the current discussion, is that there's an unseen force driving the narrative around AI safety, and it's- it's really this millenarian doomsday cult meets messianic complex called effective altruism. The most famous effective altruist that most Americans know is Sam Bankman-Fried, and the effective altruists are, it's almost like a religion that they've been thinking about doomsday scenarios from AI since the early 2000s.
MARGARET BRENNAN:  He was–he is jailed. He was the crypto investor—
SHYAM SANKAR: Correct.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who defrauded investors. But this sounds very academic. Like, what makes you so focused on this?

SHYAM SANKAR:  Because there's only really roughly 2,000 AI researchers in America, and the vast majority of them believe in this sort of worldview around effective altruism. And if you hear someone like Jacob Coxon telling you that AI has a 10% chance of ending humanity, and you believe—
MARGARET BRENNAN:  A researcher who had this warning recently.

SHYAM SANKAR: Yes, correct. And you believe he's speaking as a technically informed individual who does this work, it's a scientific critique. I think the American people would be right to be quite panicked and worried about what's going on here. But if you understand that it's actually a theological critique, then you can- you can kind of weigh it against the empirical facts of what is actually happening out there. You know, I take—I think there's a profound truth to Pascal's saying that every human has a god-shaped hole in their heart, and it's important to understand that many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine God of AGI. And I mean, there's so many interesting stories around this. Like, for example, so many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI. I believe so much— (CROSSTALK)
MARGARET BRENNAN:  What? That makes no sense. What do you think—

SHYAM SANKAR: I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I will—I'm showing you my chips are all in. So there is kind of this mass psychosis, social delusion around it, and I think it's getting in the way of actually what is happening with AI. Where is it meeting the American worker in industry? What are the results of doing that, and the doomsdayers have basically been wrong. Everything they predicted, they- they told us that ChatGPT 2.0 was too dangerous to release. They told us at this point in the timeline, we'd already have mass unemployment and job displacement, and the economists see that actually we're having job growth in areas that we wouldn't have predicted doing exactly that. So the technology industry has two burdens. One is to show very clearly to the American people that- that AI is going to result in economic prosperity and security for the nation. And two, to actually do and absorb the burden of engineering. You cannot abdicate this idea that designing safe products is your job. You can't hand wave around it. If you look at the kind of narratives that come out of the doomsdayers, they seem like two contradictory narratives. One narrative is this technology is going to end humanity.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

SHYAM SANKAR: And simultaneously, they say, "But I believe it has some chance of creating utopia." So at first blush, this seems contradictory, but it has one thing in common, which is that you, as a human, have no agency. The machine god is going to decide the future, and only perhaps a small number of us can try to avoid the horrible outcome. And I think it obfuscates the more profound reality that we have a huge amount of human agency over how we're going to use this technology to deliver the outcomes the American people expect.

MARGARET BRENNAN:  Well let's talk about that because the other part of this argument would be, and no one who wants- the people who don't want guardrails are simply in it for commercial reasons. They want to keep selling chips, or they just want access to market. So that would be the counter argument to the idea that you know what you're saying, which is an ideological opposition to guardrails.
SHYAM SANKAR: Maybe we could just back up and who's on the side of no guardrails?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when- I want to get into the specifics here, because even just defining what guardrails is seems really complicated, and there's not even common agreement on that right now. But Jay Clayton, who is the new DNI and the new AI czar, said this week the focus is on control and monitoring of technologies with the potential to do harm. So, what does that look like to you? Because it sounds like he's not even sure yet.

SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I think there's a very clear view that we should be regulating the application of the technology. So if you're going to use this in medicines, you know the FDA- As a republic, we have 250 years of rich laws and history on how to manage liability. I don't want to trivialize the metaphor, but you know, if I buy a car and the car is defective, that's the car maker's problem. If I then use that car to go drive into my neighbor's house, that's my problem. And you know, this sort of obfuscation. The narrative is this technology is a total difference of kind. I don't think so. I think it's a difference of degree.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, in that humans aren't in control of it, it would be a different kind.

SHYAM SANKAR: No, humans are in control of it. Even if we look at the kind of salacious reporting around Hugging Face, the models did not do anything they were not instructed to do. You know, they were- the- the real first, you have human error. They- they were not in a sandbox. They had access to the internet. It was a horrible cybersecurity configuration. MARGARET BRENNAN: So, for that, who should take action to--
SHYAM SANKAR: --I think it's a defective product. Like, if--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Is it up to the Justice Department to then bring suit, like on the programmers, like who's liable for the technology not, you know, staying within the sandbox--

SHYAM SANKAR: I think it is a massive running head start. I think the laws on the books speak to a lot of the current considerations. Might we need a few more things on the margin? Sure, but I think we'll figure that out as we go through it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, what happened? Like, what was the conversation?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because it sounded like the White House was saying something more should be done, and now you have this new AI Czar Jay Clayton going out to Silicon Valley this week. He said he's launched this 120-day review of AI policy. What do you hope comes from that, or is this another one of these like blue ribbon commissions that doesn't produce any--

I think one of the challenges, going back to my comments on effective altruism is, today, the so-called independent research organizations that are overseeing this are not really independent. They have conflicts with the labs. They are made up of people with a singular worldview around effective altruism, looking for the doomsday scenarios. You know, you have evaluators who are essentially pointing a loaded gun at a target, saying, "I can't believe the gun worked." When they should really be saying, "What guardrails do we have in place? You know- are you know are these products working to the specifications we designed, and what- what are the opportunities for misuse?

MARGARET BRENNAN: So I've spoken to people, for example, in the financial industry who say we did need some regulation here, but there's the SEC, there is you know the CFTC, they oversee certain operations here. Don't you think within the current institutions there could be some sort of entity that oversees technology?

SHYAM SANKAR: I think there's going to need to be an incident response and reporting regime that creates more visibility and transparency into what you're learning in the testing, well ahead of product launches that give visibility and transparency to the government of how people are doing and implementing exactly the existing laws.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who does that, or who could do that?
SHYAM SANKAR: I will defer to Director Clayton on that, but I think that's one of the things that I- I suspect they will be driving towards.

MARGARET BRENNAN: He's got to figure that out. MARGARET BRENNAN: But in terms of the things where you think there should be more guardrails, is the defense space one of them? Biotech, I've heard others.
SHYAM SANKAR: All spaces need to- need to have a thought around safety of application.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But that's still- who does that and how?

It is your alpha. It is what makes your institution special.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you don't know yet who's going to replace them, but you don't see a big impact from this kind of decision. It was certainly a huge story for Silicon Valley and the defense space to hear that--

SHYAM SANKAR: It's already been replaced. It's already been replaced, and users who are building AI applications get to pick the models that they're using. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, I was asking about the impact. It sounds like you don't think it's- it's a big one. Look, I can move on here.

blocks.text: Apple Newsroom, Tuesday morning:

The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting
users control what they’re watching and discover new shows
completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently
isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver
crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio
is playing.
This is nice, but I don’t think it buys me anything, because my existing Apple TV 4K is paired with 2nd-gen HomePods, and the HomePods each have a “four-microphone design for far-field Siri”.

The A19 chip in the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent
faster CPU performance and up to 2× faster GPU performance than
the previous generation, for greater responsiveness, faster
navigation, and smoother animations. The A19 chip also includes a
new, dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality
streaming while using less bandwidth.

The new AV1 decoder seems like it might be meaningful, but does anyone think UI navigation and animation smoothness is improved by going from the A15 to the A19 SoC? I mean navigation is going up/down/left/right. I’m sure the graphics and CPU improvements matter for gaming, but the only mention of gaming in Apple’s own Newsroom announcement is this sentence: “With Apple Fitness+, the living room becomes a workout studio, while Apple Arcade and the App Store’s library of games turn it into a home arcade.” I wish it were otherwise, but gaming is such an afterthought on Apple TV that it only garnered the second half of a sentence that started with Fitness+, a service that has only been in the news this year because Mark Gurman says Apple laid off part of the team.

The new Siri Remote keeps its familiar design while adding Find My
support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound on
the remote — making it far easier to locate.

That’s my single favorite feature in the announcement. I hate to say it though, but the previous remote should have supported these features. The 3rd-gen Apple TV 4K came in 2022, but Apple launched AirTags with Precision Finding in 2021. Remote controls are right after keys on the list of things people misplace most frequently, and Apple’s remote controls, because they’re small and thin, are particularly susceptible to being snatched by couch-cushion gremlins. Speakers, so the remote can play a sound to help you find it, were invented even earlier than 2021.

Pairing HomePod with Apple TV 4K already offers users an immersive
viewing experience that’s easy to set up, and the new Apple TV 4K
takes it even further. For the first time, users can create a
four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th
generation) and HomePod mini 2. The four speakers work together
with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the
room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to
the space. HomePod (2nd generation) can also be used in this
four-speaker setup for the ultimate audio experience, as long as
the front and rear speaker pairs match.
This is tempting to try. In other words, in addition to the two 2nd-gen HomePods I already have paired in my living room, I can add two of the new HomePod Mini 2’s behind the sofa for surround sound.

The elephant in the room, though, is price. Before this week, Apple sold two models of the 3rd-generation Apple TV. On a percentage basis, they were hit the hardest of any products Apple sells by the company’s across-the-board price increases this summer:

The new Apple TV 4K announced this week only comes in one model, and it costs $300. It’s great that there’s only one model for simplicity’s sake, but the number one complaint when the previous generation cost $130/150 was that it was too expensive compared to set-top boxes and sticks from Amazon and Roku. (Or the “free” option of using the “smart TV” software that comes with every TV set.) Now, with the new Apple TV, it’s twice as expensive — and Apple is not keeping the 3rd-gen models around as lower-priced options. I still think it’s worth it, personally, but the general consumer market thought the old prices were too high and I don’t see any of the new features making Joe or Jane Consumer think, “Sure, I was skeptical about the old one at $130, but this new model — which looks exactly the same — this seems worth $300.”

HomePod Mini 2 now costs $150. That’s not too much of an increase over the new-since-June-25 $130 price for the old HomePod Mini, but it’s a stiff 50 percent increase from the old HomePod Mini’s $100 price from November 2020 through June 24 this year. I generally round Apple’s prices up from their “99” values, but it’s worth noting that what I’m calling $100 was actually $99, and going to just two digits does have a psychological effect on buying behavior. Again, I think $150 is a reasonable price for the HomePod Mini 2, but it doesn’t feel as much like a lark as $99 did. $99 was a bit of a “Sure, let’s get another one” price; $150 is more of a “Do we really need another one of these?” price.

At the old pre-June prices, you could buy a 128 GB Apple TV and a pair of HomePod Minis for $350 ($150 + $100 + $100). Four short months later, with today’s new models, that combination would cost $600 ($300 + $150 + $150). That price difference is much more striking than any of the new and improved features in the products.

blocks.text: As I mentioned before, it takes me way too long to edit a single video. So I am releasing it in chunks. If I never finish it, well then at least I'll have a few videos out.

What is the video about? Well, it is about the future we were promised, versus the one we are actually living in. It's not dystopian, but it seems like the goal of tech is supposedly to automate the tedious and mundane, so we can have more time to do the things we love. But along the way came the word productivity. The goal of productivity is not to get free time. It is to produce more in the same amount of time. Not produce more in less time. Read this a couple times for it to stick.

You find the weirdest stuff inside your walls. Our house was built in 1949 and we're its third owner, and I have no idea what those other people were doing, but at one point someone installed a junction box full of live, bare wires that they filled with crumpled newspaper (!); and don't get me started on the decision not to put vapor barriers in the kitchen windows (we were one good shake away from the entire front of the house falling down when we discovered that one, and while it cost us an extra $19,000 to fix, that was still cheaper than rebuilding the whole front of the house).

Plus there was the unpermitted drainage system installed down the side of the house that must have attracted some (undocumented) planning inspector negativity; at least, that's the only reason I can think of for someone to have filled those drains with concrete (!!), a fact we discovered during the first heavy rainfall after moving in, when the water rose to shin-height (!!!).

But the weirdest and most nerve-wracking mysteries were the "structural" members of dubious quality, placement and utility. Some of them only seemed to be holding stuff up, but on closer inspection turned out to be free-floating 2x4s, not anchored to anything. On more than one occasion, our builders have moved jacks into position and removed those random uprights, only to discover that they weren't holding anything up.
Say what you will about this method, but it is decisive: if you remove a vertical member and nothing falls down, you can be pretty sure that wasn't a load-bearing member.
(This is a metaphor about AI.)

You can be forgiven for rolling your eyes when the subject of "digital sovereignty" comes up. Rhetorically, "digital sovereignty" is a coded way for a politician to say, "We should build a fuckton of AI data-centers while bypassing any environmental review":
https://datacentremagazine.com/technology-and-ai/keir-starmers-2bn-pledge-how-the-uk-plans-to-advance-ai

But AI has nothing to do with digital sovereignty. It is not load-bearing. All it takes to understand this is a little thought-experiment. Imagine that we removed all the chatbots from Canada, or the UK, or the EU, or the USA. What would fall down?
Nothing important.

Every public administrative body – national, regional and local – would continue to function. Every firm – large and small – would continue to trade. Households would be unscathed, save for their youngest members, who would suffer the indignity and tedium of having to do their own homework again.

Which is not to say that "digital sovereignty" is a nothingburger. The walls of our nations are filled with load-bearing digital members. It's just that these are the most boring, regular-degular-ass technologies imaginable.
Like Microsoft Office 365. Take away M365 and every ministry collapses, every firm shutters, and many if not most households will be in serious trouble.
And here's the thing: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella paid $1m out of his own pocket to join the murderer's row of tech CEOs who sat behind Trump on the inaugural dais:
https://apnews.com/article/trump-inauguration-tech-billionaires-zuckerberg-musk-wealth-0896bfc3f50d941d62cebc3074267ecd
Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump's Epstein Memorial Ballroom:
https://www.geekwire.com/2026/leaked-list-shows-what-microsoft-amazon-and-other-tech-giants-are-giving-for-the-white-house-ballroom/
Microsoft provides the back-end administrative infrastructure for Trump's racist pogroms (take away M365 and ICE would collapse):
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/17/ice-microsoft-technology-immigration-crackdown
The CEO of Microsoft France admitted that if Trump ordered the company to spy on French citizens' data (or the data of the French government), his company would comply, in secret:
https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/

And here's the kicker: Microsoft has terminated the M365 and Outlook access of international public officials whose official acts made Trump angry, starting with the Chief Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, who lost his accounts after he swore out the genocide warrant for Netanyahu:
https://www.computerweekly.com/opinion/Microsofts-ICC-email-block-reignites-European-data-sovereignty-concerns

This is a white-hot, 278-alarm digital sovereignty dumpster-fire. M365 – as well as cloud software from Oracle, Google, Apple, Amazon and other US tech giants that have fused themselves with the Trump regime in exchange for tax breaks and antitrust forbearance – is load-bearing, and worse, those 2x4s are filled with termites and dry-rot.
Digital sovereignty is as real as real can be. It just has nothing to do with AI. AI isn't load-bearing. Boring-ass tech monopolist cloud software is…and we can not trust it:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

blocks.text: It's hard to craft a book with so much righteous indignation - let alone make it funny, accessible, and informative. Nevertheless, Dipo Faloyin has succeeded in writing a spectacular takedown of the myths which are often perpetrated about Africa.
It starts in the best way possible:

[Insert generic African proverb here. Ideally an allegory about a wise monkey and his interaction with a tree, or the relationship between the donkey and the ant that surprisingly speaks to grand gestures of valour. Sign it off: Ancient African proverb]
How many times have you seen that? Think about all the tropes played out in every Hollywood movie set vaguely in Africa - would you accept the same stereotypes about your continent?
And yet, it does rely a little too much about internalised stereotypes:
The point is: there are a lot of people in Lagos. None of them are shy.
I'm sure there's at least one introvert in Lagos who cringes every time people expect them to be boisterous!

The horrors and complexities of colonisation and its aftermath are on display for all to see. In many way, much like cryptobros discovering why banking regulations exist, some African countries are speed-running Europe's history of bloody internecine warfare and mad kings. A predilection that some parts of Europe (and America) are still struggling to move past.

I think it could have benefited from just a few maps or illustrations. I also found some of the language a little… infantilising? The way he capitalises certain phrases like "These Powerful Men In The Capital" felt to me a little out of place. That said, there's some excellent caustic humour and some quite beautiful prose.

In the end, it shows that while Africa is not a country, the stories are often of different countries tackling the same problems in the same ways. [Insert something about everyone's hearts beating to the rhythm of an African drum, while an elephant wanders into an impossibly huge sunset.]

articles.title: C++ futures part 5: std::future and std::shared_future
articles.titleZh: C++ futures part 5: std::future and std::shared_future
articles.summary: C++ futures part 5: std::future and std::shared_future

blocks.text: Wrapping up our quick introduction to the C++ futures library, we come to the last two parts: std::future and std::shared_future.
The std::future is the starting point. It is a move-only class that this takes the source and forwards its wait and wait_for methods to the source, and forwards its get method to consume.
Forwarding the get to consume means that you can call get only once.

The idea is that std::future is for the case where there is exactly one consumer of the value. Since it is move-only, you can’t copy it; you can only give it away and transfer the power to retrieve the value to the recipient.

The std::future has a method called shared(). This transfers the source from the future to a shared_future object. The shared_future also forwards its wait and wait_for methods to the source, but instead of forwarding its get to the source::consume, shared_future::get() just calls source::get to get a reference to the value storage.

This is what makes the “shared future” shared: The shared_future is copyable, so you can have multiple people all with their own shared_future that share the same source, and each one can separately wait for the value and retrieve the value as many times as they want.

The downside of shared_future is that you always get a const reference, so if you want to perform non-const operations on the result, you’ll have to make a copy and operate on the copy. And that’s not possible at all if the result is itself a move-only type, since you can’t move out of a const reference.

You can see that at the end of the day, all of the pieces of the futures library are just different ways of manipulating the invisible source. Some components push values into the source, and others pull values out of the source.
It took me a while to realize that the most important part of the whole futures library is something you can’t even see.
Bonus chatter: All the names in the futures library are horrible. I mean, really, “packaged task”?
Here’s my attempt to give the pieces better names:

I admit, these names aren’t all that good either. But I prefer to use the word “promise” to refer to the thing that “promises” to produce a value. And the pattern promise_source / promise makes the relationship between the two much clearer: A promise source is a thing that makes promises. And it avoids the hilarity of a non-async async().

blocks.text: This post began as a thread on X last night. I’ve edited the thread to turn it into a blog post, making some additions and corrections.
I’m watching 2010: The Year We Make Contact. The movie opens saying the monolith is located at the Lagrange point between Jupiter and Io. I got nerd sniped and wondered where that was.

There are five Lagrange points, but presumably the movie refers to L1 or L2 because these are near Io. Lagrange points L3, L4, and L5 are essentially in the orbit of Io, but 60, 180, and 300 degrees out of phase, all far from Io. (The book says the monolith is at L1.)
Lagrange points L1 and L2 are unstable. Maybe this is a plot hole in the movie, unless there’s an explanation coming.

(In general L1, L2, and L3 are unstable. If the ratio of the masses is large enough, L4 and L5 will be stable. More on that here. The Lagrange points L4 and L5 are indeed stable for the Jupiter-Io system. For the Sun-Earth system L1 is moderately stable over a short time span, but L1 is far less stable for the Jupiter-Io system.)
Here’s a plot of the Lagrange points.
Note that L1 and L2 are very close to Io, about 10,000 km from the moon. The L1 and L2 Lagrange points for the Earth-Sun system are not so close to Earth.

(That’s half true. Yes, Io’s L1 point is closer to it than Earth’s L1 point, in absolute distance. But in relative terms, Io’s L1 point is actually further away. I had been mislead by seeing an illustration that exaggerated the distance from Earth to L1.)

blocks.text: Soundtrack: Spinnerette — A Prescription For Mankind

About fourteen years ago, the government made a mistake that would allow tech companies and venture capitalists to conspire to legally scam millions of retail investors, simultaneously depriving them of good information and spuriously inflating the valuations of every major tech IPO of the last 14 years.

On April 5, 2012, President Obama signed the Jumpstart Our Business Startups (JOBS) Act under the auspices of it being “too difficult” for small businesses and startups — though overwhelmingly the latter — to access capital, all while reducing reporting requirements in ways that mostly helped venture capitalists fund and startup founders run businesses in reckless and destructive ways, all sold as a good thing for society.

In simple terms, while the JOBS Act (which was passed with rare bipartisan support) allowed companies to raise more money from more people, it also incentivized companies staying private for longer by eliminating a rule from the 60s that required companies of a certain size — above 500 shareholders and $10 million in assets — to report as if they were public.
[Editor's Note: It said "public for longer," that's now been fixed.]
Per Casual Finance:

In 1964, Congress implemented a rule to securities law called Section 12(g)...[which] said that once a company of any real size had 500 shareholders, it had to start reporting like a public company. This acted as a trigger that pushed private companies into a public reporting regime - the same way a public company reports its financials, a private company would have to file quarterly reports, an annual report, and an update every time something big happened - which was a huge deal for startups, because startups pay people in stock. Every employee who got shares instead of a bigger paycheck was one more shareholder on the way to 500.

As Casual Finance notes, this is the rule that pushed both Facebook and Google to go public — because if you’re going to have to report like a public company, you may as well have access to the public markets:

Back in 2010, Zuck flat out said it. "We aren't planning to go public anytime soon." Then he continued by saying “I tend to think that being private is better for us right now because of some of the big risks we want to take in developing new products.And Facebook didn't need the money. They were the hottest startup in the world and everyone wanted in…which is how, in January 2011, Facebook announced it had just raised $1.5 billion privately.But in that same announcement, Facebook said it expected to pass 500 shareholders sometime that year. Which meant they would have to start publishing their financials "no later than April 30, 2012."So Facebook was about to get the worst of both worlds.They were about to have to put their numbers out in the open for every competitor to be able to read, just like a public company. Without any of the upside of actually being a public company. Like a large infusion of equity capital and having liquidity for your stock.So in 2012, Facebook took their stock public.

The JOBS act, amongst other changes, made it so that you could have up to 2,000 shareholders (but no more than 499 “unaccredited” investors) and, crucially, changed the rules so that employees were no longer counted in the calculation, effectively removing any chance that most startups would ever have to deal with reporting like a public company ever again.

The rationale was that having to report like a public company required audited accounts, adding an "unnecessary burden” to fledgling companies, even though “fledgling” here meant “companies worth hundreds of billions of dollars on paper” that absolutely could afford an auditor. Those pushing for the bill also believed that these requirements unfairly punished companies for awarding stock grants, and that public reporting was tantamount to “exposing trade secrets,” as if there was literally no amendment that could’ve been made to anticipate these problems other than “removing reporting anything of any sort.”

However minor this change might have seemed at the time, the net result was one of the largest private valuation bubbles in history, because there was (and is) no longer any incentive for a company to go public before it’s “ready,” with “ready” defined as “as much value has been drained from the company as humanely possible.”

As Casual Finance noted, when Microsoft went public, it had a market cap of around $500 million, Google $23 billion, and Facebook $100 billion, with their total market capitalization as of writing this sentence sitting at around $10.29 trillion. Anyone investing in any of these IPOs in the first five to ten years of their existence had a chance to multiply their money, because you were able to invest before the companies became massive multiconglomerates with multi-trillion dollar market caps, in turn creating value for millions of households that “took the risk” on investing on an earlier-stage company.

These three companies are used as the poster children of why you should invest in a new tech stock — that you’re getting in on the ground floor, with the reward for the risk being that you’d have the chance of a massive multiple.
Except that doesn’t really work if the companies wait as long as humanly possible to go public.

The reason that Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon and all the other famous names in “big IPOs that made early investors a lot of money” was that they had to go public before they’d reached the height of their valuation.
And crucially, their valuations are decided by market forces which, while deranged and emotional, at least are somewhat guided by the underlying financial picture of the company.

Today’s startups have their valuations defined entirely based on the whims and fancies of a venture capital sect that makes up a multiple they’re comfortable investing at. That’s how Instinct, a zero-revenue “AI agent” that you text to do stuff, is somehow worth $10 billion — because investors from Sequoia Capital, Benchmark, and Coatue had been willing to give it $1 billion for 10% of the company.

These inflated valuations drain the vast majority of potential opportunity that any investor might have, effectively transferring all the risk for the company’s future onto the public markets while offering very little in return. The days of thousand-percent-or-more returns are long dead, despite every single IPO selling itself on this eventuality, like SpaceX did when it proposed it had a $28.5 trillion total addressable market.

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO has the company demanding a $2 trillion valuation, equivalent to both Meta and SpaceX, based on flimsy promises of $200 billion in annual revenue years in the future and a $30 trillion total addressable market. It is, to quote New Constructs, presenting risks and is positioned to be a far bigger ripoff of the US capital markets, and exists only as a liquidity mechanism so that early investors can multiply their dodgily-valued early investments by selling their shares under the scummiest possible terms.

Anthropic and OpenAI’s IPOs pose a genuine threat to any investor that dares entangle themselves with unprofitable, unsustainable AI companies promising the world (or the world’s destruction), all sold under the auspices of potentially buying into the next Facebook, Google or Microsoft. In reality, the kind of growth you’d need from these companies to reach anything close to the returns of those early-stage tech investments would require them to have trillions of dollars a year in revenue and market capitalizations of $20 trillion or more — an impossibility that nobody seems to want to discuss.
Yet these rotten incentives have also led to a massive valuation bubble in startup valuations writ large, with the AI bubble being the inevitable result.

By allowing private companies to avoid the reporting strictures of the public markets, financial regulations incentivize a kind of venture welfare, keeping companies that cannot borrow money or otherwise sustain themselves through cashflow — you know, bad companies — alive for longer than is natural, never forcing them to become real companies that can survive, with every trip to Sand Hill Road bumping the valuation up further, making any IPO or acquisition much harder to stomach.

This wasn’t as much of a problem when venture capital was pumping up software companies and flogging them to the markets or dimwitted private equity firms, but has become a critical situation for the legions of cashflow-negative AI companies with aggressively-inflated valuations.

In a pre-JOBS environment, many of these companies would’ve wilted in sunlight, and, I’d argue, been forced to run businesses that could stand on their own two feet. Instead, as I discussed in last year’s Enshittifinancial Crisis, these companies are more venture-dependent than any other hype cycle in history, and because venture is so excited about the potential, they’re investing at bigger and bigger rounds, creating the largest valuation bubble in the history of technology, including the Dot Com Bubble.
Today I am going to aggressively advocate for reforms — if not an outright repeal — of the JOBS act, and call for serious legislative efforts to bring the private markets to heel.

My argument is simple: the current system is built to incentivize rich and powerful people inflating private assets with spurious valuations, harming retail investors, reducing the available capital to good startups, and incentivizing the continued development of bad, unsustainable companies. Venture is no longer a trustworthy vehicle for investment, nor can venture capitalists be trusted to value startups any further.

The JOBS act did the literal opposite of what it intended to — fewer tech companies went public, and those that went public did so at oversized valuations pumped up by venture capital, using retail investors as exit liquidity under the flimsy pretense of “getting in on the ground floor.” We are placing outsized trust in a handful of extremely rich and disconnected people and their ability to pick winners, despite the fact that the majority of venture capitalists are fucking terrible at doing so.

For over a decade, venture capital has inflated the value of startup after startup, then been surprised again and again as these companies didn’t work out, with the vast majority of “successes” — SpaceX, Snap, Airbnb, and Uber — mostly existing to dump their horrid bags on an unsuspecting public.
And by repeating the same cycle — inflating companies based on hype and ever-growing valuations — venture capital is setting itself up for a collapse.
Today I’ll explain how it’s happening, and how we might fix what’s left in the end.

About fourteen years ago, the government made a mistake that would allow tech companies and venture capitalists to conspire to legally scam millions of retail investors, simultaneously depriving them of good information and spuriously inflating the valuations of every major tech IPO of the last 14 years.

On April 5, 2012, President Obama signed the Jumpstart Our Business Startups (JOBS) Act under the auspices of it being “too difficult” for small businesses and startups — though overwhelmingly the latter — to access capital, all while reducing reporting requirements in ways that mostly helped venture capitalists fund and startup founders run businesses in reckless and destructive ways, all sold as a good thing for society.

In simple terms, while the JOBS Act (which was passed with rare bipartisan support) allowed companies to raise more money from more people, it also incentivized companies staying private for longer by eliminating a rule from the 60s that required companies of a certain size — above 500 shareholders and $10 million in assets — to report as if they were public.
[Editor's Note: It said "public for longer," that's now been fixed.]
Per Casual Finance:

In 1964, Congress implemented a rule to securities law called Section 12(g)...[which] said that once a company of any real size had 500 shareholders, it had to start reporting like a public company. This acted as a trigger that pushed private companies into a public reporting regime - the same way a public company reports its financials, a private company would have to file quarterly reports, an annual report, and an update every time something big happened - which was a huge deal for startups, because startups pay people in stock. Every employee who got shares instead of a bigger paycheck was one more shareholder on the way to 500.

As Casual Finance notes, this is the rule that pushed both Facebook and Google to go public — because if you’re going to have to report like a public company, you may as well have access to the public markets:

Back in 2010, Zuck flat out said it. "We aren't planning to go public anytime soon." Then he continued by saying “I tend to think that being private is better for us right now because of some of the big risks we want to take in developing new products.And Facebook didn't need the money. They were the hottest startup in the world and everyone wanted in…which is how, in January 2011, Facebook announced it had just raised $1.5 billion privately.But in that same announcement, Facebook said it expected to pass 500 shareholders sometime that year. Which meant they would have to start publishing their financials "no later than April 30, 2012."So Facebook was about to get the worst of both worlds.They were about to have to put their numbers out in the open for every competitor to be able to read, just like a public company. Without any of the upside of actually being a public company. Like a large infusion of equity capital and having liquidity for your stock.So in 2012, Facebook took their stock public.

The JOBS act, amongst other changes, made it so that you could have up to 2,000 shareholders (but no more than 499 “unaccredited” investors) and, crucially, changed the rules so that employees were no longer counted in the calculation, effectively removing any chance that most startups would ever have to deal with reporting like a public company ever again.

The rationale was that having to report like a public company required audited accounts, adding an "unnecessary burden” to fledgling companies, even though “fledgling” here meant “companies worth hundreds of billions of dollars on paper” that absolutely could afford an auditor. Those pushing for the bill also believed that these requirements unfairly punished companies for awarding stock grants, and that public reporting was tantamount to “exposing trade secrets,” as if there was literally no amendment that could’ve been made to anticipate these problems other than “removing reporting anything of any sort.”

However minor this change might have seemed at the time, the net result was one of the largest private valuation bubbles in history, because there was (and is) no longer any incentive for a company to go public before it’s “ready,” with “ready” defined as “as much value has been drained from the company as humanely possible.”

As Casual Finance noted, when Microsoft went public, it had a market cap of around $500 million, Google $23 billion, and Facebook $100 billion, with their total market capitalization as of writing this sentence sitting at around $10.29 trillion. Anyone investing in any of these IPOs in the first five to ten years of their existence had a chance to multiply their money, because you were able to invest before the companies became massive multiconglomerates with multi-trillion dollar market caps, in turn creating value for millions of households that “took the risk” on investing on an earlier-stage company.

These three companies are used as the poster children of why you should invest in a new tech stock — that you’re getting in on the ground floor, with the reward for the risk being that you’d have the chance of a massive multiple.
Except that doesn’t really work if the companies wait as long as humanly possible to go public.

The reason that Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon and all the other famous names in “big IPOs that made early investors a lot of money” was that they had to go public before they’d reached the height of their valuation.
And crucially, their valuations are decided by market forces which, while deranged and emotional, at least are somewhat guided by the underlying financial picture of the company.

Today’s startups have their valuations defined entirely based on the whims and fancies of a venture capital sect that makes up a multiple they’re comfortable investing at. That’s how Instinct, a zero-revenue “AI agent” that you text to do stuff, is somehow worth $10 billion — because investors from Sequoia Capital, Benchmark, and Coatue had been willing to give it $1 billion for 10% of the company.

These inflated valuations drain the vast majority of potential opportunity that any investor might have, effectively transferring all the risk for the company’s future onto the public markets while offering very little in return. The days of thousand-percent-or-more returns are long dead, despite every single IPO selling itself on this eventuality, like SpaceX did when it proposed it had a $28.5 trillion total addressable market.

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO has the company demanding a $2 trillion valuation, equivalent to both Meta and SpaceX, based on flimsy promises of $200 billion in annual revenue years in the future and a $30 trillion total addressable market. It is, to quote New Constructs, presenting risks and is positioned to be a far bigger ripoff of the US capital markets, and exists only as a liquidity mechanism so that early investors can multiply their dodgily-valued early investments by selling their shares under the scummiest possible terms.

Anthropic and OpenAI’s IPOs pose a genuine threat to any investor that dares entangle themselves with unprofitable, unsustainable AI companies promising the world (or the world’s destruction), all sold under the auspices of potentially buying into the next Facebook, Google or Microsoft. In reality, the kind of growth you’d need from these companies to reach anything close to the returns of those early-stage tech investments would require them to have trillions of dollars a year in revenue and market capitalizations of $20 trillion or more — an impossibility that nobody seems to want to discuss.
Yet these rotten incentives have also led to a massive valuation bubble in startup valuations writ large, with the AI bubble being the inevitable result.

By allowing private companies to avoid the reporting strictures of the public markets, financial regulations incentivize a kind of venture welfare, keeping companies that cannot borrow money or otherwise sustain themselves through cashflow — you know, bad companies — alive for longer than is natural, never forcing them to become real companies that can survive, with every trip to Sand Hill Road bumping the valuation up further, making any IPO or acquisition much harder to stomach.

This wasn’t as much of a problem when venture capital was pumping up software companies and flogging them to the markets or dimwitted private equity firms, but has become a critical situation for the legions of cashflow-negative AI companies with aggressively-inflated valuations.

In a pre-JOBS environment, many of these companies would’ve wilted in sunlight, and, I’d argue, been forced to run businesses that could stand on their own two feet. Instead, as I discussed in last year’s Enshittifinancial Crisis, these companies are more venture-dependent than any other hype cycle in history, and because venture is so excited about the potential, they’re investing at bigger and bigger rounds, creating the largest valuation bubble in the history of technology, including the Dot Com Bubble.
Today I am going to aggressively advocate for reforms — if not an outright repeal — of the JOBS act, and call for serious legislative efforts to bring the private markets to heel.

My argument is simple: the current system is built to incentivize rich and powerful people inflating private assets with spurious valuations, harming retail investors, reducing the available capital to good startups, and incentivizing the continued development of bad, unsustainable companies. Venture is no longer a trustworthy vehicle for investment, nor can venture capitalists be trusted to value startups any further.

The JOBS act did the literal opposite of what it intended to — fewer tech companies went public, and those that went public did so at oversized valuations pumped up by venture capital, using retail investors as exit liquidity under the flimsy pretense of “getting in on the ground floor.” We are placing outsized trust in a handful of extremely rich and disconnected people and their ability to pick winners, despite the fact that the majority of venture capitalists are fucking terrible at doing so.

For over a decade, venture capital has inflated the value of startup after startup, then been surprised again and again as these companies didn’t work out, with the vast majority of “successes” — SpaceX, Snap, Airbnb, and Uber — mostly existing to dump their horrid bags on an unsuspecting public.
And by repeating the same cycle — inflating companies based on hype and ever-growing valuations — venture capital is setting itself up for a collapse.
Today I’ll explain how it’s happening, and how we might fix what’s left in the end.

On October 16, 1995, Roland Vossen accidentally invented spyware in a Usenet post. Well, not exactly. He didn’t invent spyware so much as he invented the term. His Usenet post contained the first recorded use of the word “spyware.”

For context, his post contained about 150 lines of pseudocode, making fun of Microsoft’s release cycles, marketing hype, and other aspects of its business model. One of the include statements in the code referenced a file called spyware.h. It was in close proximity to lines that referenced files called lies.h and nonsense.h.

If only Roland Vossen knew how prophetic his parody was. My blog post on defeating the spying mechanisms in Windows 11 is fairly popular. Every consumer operating system today is spyware to one degree or another.

Things got a lot worse before they got better. And I’m not quite sure that “better” would be the right word, because spyware never really went away. It just takes a different form now than it did in the ’90s.
Spyware in the ’90s

In the ’90s, a very popular business model was giving stuff away for free and then trying to figure out how to make money off it. Geocities‘ business model was giving away web hosting. Mark Cuban’s Broadcast.com gave away regional radio broadcasts. But my favorite extreme case is Cyberrebate. Cyberrebate gave away actual physical merchandise. I remember going into a guy’s office in late 1998 or early 1999, and he showed me this box of junk he’d just received for free. Well, it wasn’t exactly free. It was an online store that promised 100% rebates. So you had to fill out a bunch of paperwork, mail it in within a certain length of time, not make any mistakes, and wait months for the rebate check to arrive. But if you were willing to do all of that, you could get a bunch of trinkets for free.
This was more than 25 years ago but I remember it like it was yesterday. The absurdity of someone being so excited about getting a $6 laser pointer for free stuck with me.

A majority of people never send the rebate paperwork in, and some additional percentage mess it up. But this particular company grossly underestimated how many people would put in the effort to get it right, especially if they had ordered a large amount.
The business model of giving away software

Giving away actual physical merchandise was an extreme example, however. A much more common business model was giving away software. People would write a useful or just fun piece of software, and then monetize it by injecting a couple of DLLs into it. Sometimes these DLLs collected telemetry that was useful to marketers, sometimes it just displayed random ads, and some of it did both. Whoever provided them the DLLs paid them based on the results they delivered, so the more popular your program was, the more money you’d make from the spyware.

Some of it behaved really poorly too. The telltale sign of where the ads were coming from was when something called advert.dll would crash and Windows would give you a message that it had shut it down.
I knew when people were infected when I got help desk tickets complaining that users were seeing ads on internal websites.

After Napster got sued out of business, companies who decided they wanted to enter the file sharing business realized they needed to have a revenue stream just in case they got sued. So they included spyware along with their file sharing client.

The problem with this business model was too many people were doing it. A system would get loaded down with too much spyware, and the system would start failing to do seemingly unrelated tasks until it became essentially unusable.

The problem got so bad that an entire product category sprung up to fight it. You didn’t necessarily just need antivirus software. You needed anti-spyware software. Anti-spyware didn’t need to do realtime scanning like antivirus software at least. It was sufficient to just run a scan on a weekly or monthly basis or whenever your system was misbehaving. I even had a blog post telling people how to fix a system just enough so they could run antispyware tools.
It was a scandal when Lenovo shipped systems with spyware pre-installed a decade ago.
When enough people started using anti-spyware software, companies started looking for other more sustainable sources of revenue.

The exception being the operating system vendors. All of the mainstream operating systems are spyware. No, Linux and FreeBSD are not mainstream operating systems, at least not on the desktop. Microsoft does it, but it’s not just Microsoft. Apple and Google do it too.

But outside of operating systems and web browsers, traditional spyware is fairly rare today. The operating system and browser vendors have figured out how to spy on you without making your system crash. Since almost nobody notices, almost nobody complains. So when I say things like Apple, Google, and Microsoft spy on you, I sound like the one who needs a head examination. Worse yet when I say televisions spy on you.

Social media spies on you too. We voluntarily give social media companies a tremendous amount of information by interacting with businesses on their sites, reacting to the posts that we see, and they can even tell things by how long you linger on a particular post. They use this information to keep you engaged, keep you addicted, and they sell the information.

So while it seems like the spyware problem has gone away, it’s a misnomer to say the problem doesn’t exist anymore. The spyware just got much better at not causing problems that blow its cover and not getting caught. It causes different problems that most people never relate back to the original source.
But I don’t blame Roland Vossen for any of this. He was just making a joke that, in October 1995, was genuinely funny. At least to people like me.

He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
